newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Macfarlane says jobs need more than growth.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Macfarlane says jobs need more than growth.

text.p: Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) governor Ian Macfarlane said on Thursday that strong rates of economic growth did not necessarily ensure that unemployment would fall.
In a speech to the Australia-Israel Chamber of Commerce, he said there was no definite linkage between regulated labour markets and job creation.
"It seems reasonably apparent that while good economic growth is a very important part of reducing unemployment, growth alone will not be the whole answer," he said.

"If it was, Europe's unemployment rates would be much more like that of the United States. There is something in the European system which means that growth is not converted into jobs in the same way as it is in the United States," the central bank chief said.

"People who have spent a great deal of time studying these issues have come to the conclusion that the highly regulated labour markets that form part of the continental European world can often work ag ainst the interests of job creation," he said.

Macfarlane, who argued that the nation should seek sober growth rates rather levels of up to five percent which would prove unmanageable, said it had not yet been proven that reforms such as labour market changes had allowed stronger growth.

"But even though there is some tentative evidence of higher productivity, I think we have still got a lot further to go before we could be confident that supply-side reforms have significantly lifted our potential growth rate," he said.
The RBA governor said Australia's unemployment performance was unfortunately similar to that of Europe, citing common labour market institutions in some respects.

"Our labour market was never as deregulated as the United States and we have not gone through recent deregulations to the same extent as have the United Kingdom and New Zealand," he said. "Last year the government enacted some changes to increase flexibility through the Workplae Relations Act. These changes, simplifying and streamlining arrangements and making it easier to strike bargains, seem to be a move in the right direction."
But it was too early to judge how beneficial these changes would be.
Macfarlane most Australians believed the concept of equity was important in choosing policy outcomes.
"As a result, we would not want to go completely down the U.S. route, with such extreme differences in incomes between senior executives of companies and the shop floor," he said.
"All I am suggesting is that we should re-examine our labour market institutions to see whether they are protecting those in jobs at the expense of those looking for jobs."
